claims.text: The proposed process uses 10 hours of high-energy ball milling in Ar followed by SPS at 950 ± 50 °C, 100 °C/min, 3 minutes, and 50 MPa.
The proposed milling and SPS regime will produce greater than 98% theoretical density.
The proposed regime will stabilize a nanocrystalline FCC-dominant CoCrFeNiTi solid solution with a minor BCC fraction.
The resulting grain size will be below 100 nm.
HCP formation is favored at lower temperatures in Co-rich alloys because of negative stacking-fault energy.
Increasing temperature above a critical threshold makes FCC thermodynamically stable and suppresses HCP formation in CoCrFeNiTi.
Sintering above 1200 °C causes grain coarsening and Laves-phase or oxide precipitation.
A high strain rate during SPS suppresses diffusion-controlled phase separation.
A rapid thermal cycle minimizes Ti-induced oxide formation.
High SPS pressure and temperature eliminate porosity while retaining or promoting grain refinement.
The processed alloy will exhibit a Vickers hardness of 450–550 HV.
The hardness will arise primarily from Hall–Petch grain-boundary strengthening and solid-solution strengthening rather than precipitation hardening.
The final microstructure will contain 50–100 nm grains and less than 10 vol% BCC precipitates in a continuous FCC matrix.
The final bulk porosity will be below 2%.
The compressive yield strength will exceed 1200 MPa.
Conventional casting of this alloy produces a porous, soft single-phase state with hardness below 200 HV.
Milling beyond 15 hours causes excessive carbide or oxide contamination and embrittlement.
The larger atomic radius of Ti may shift the FCC-to-HCP suppression threshold relative to CoCrFeMnNi.
A Vickers test at a 0.5 kg load and 15-second dwell is proposed to evaluate hardness.
Hardness below 350 HV despite a nanocrystalline grain size would show that grain refinement is not the primary strengthening mechanism.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says elevated temperature above a critical threshold suppresses HCP by stabilizing FCC, whereas the boundary says temperatures above 1100 °C cause HCP formation and the experiment expects 1100 °C samples to have more HCP. No upper-temperature reversal mechanism is supplied.
The hypothesis specifies a heating rate greater than 100 °C/min, but the explicit intervention uses exactly 100 °C/min.
